items.title: Inventory System
items.short: A complete inventory built from scratch. A 30 slot grid, two hotbars, live 3D item viewports, per item durability, and saving that brings a worn tool back worn.
body: A complete inventory built from scratch. Items drag between a 30 slot grid and a nine slot hotbar, render as live 3D models of the real meshes, and wear down as you use them. Right clicking a slot opens a context menu to use, drop, or inspect. Everything the player sees reacts instantly, and everything that actually matters is confirmed by the server before it counts.

The system is split into services rather than one giant script. DataService owns saving and loading, InventoryService owns the rules, and RejoinService backs a !rejoin chat command that drops a player straight back into the running server. The client is broken into its own controllers for the panel, both hotbars, the drag ghost, the item viewports, tooltips, notifications, and the context menu, so no single script owns more than one job.

Shared code sits in the middle. A typed item database defines every tool once, a Signal module carries internal events without leaning on BindableEvents, and a Types module keeps the client and the server agreed on the shape of the data.
features: Drag and drop between any two slots, with a ghost that follows the cursor
Items move rather than copy, so a tool sent to the hotbar leaves the grid behind
Two hotbars, one docked in the panel for arranging and one on screen for selecting
Per item health and durability, tracked on the item itself and drawn as bars
Live 3D viewports of the real tool meshes, spinning in the grid and flat on the bar
Equipping puts the actual Tool in the character hands, replacing the default Roblox backpack
Hover tooltips, search filtering, one click sort, and a notification queue
Sound and motion feedback on every interaction
Saves to DataStore, so a worn tool comes back worn and still in its slot
architecture: Client controllers: HudController driving PanelController, HotbarController, DragController, ItemViewport, ContextMenu, Tooltip, Notifications, Motion, and UiSound
Nine dedicated remotes rather than one catch all, so every call is validated on its own terms
Every payload sent as a dense array, because Roblox remotes quietly drop sparse table keys past a gap
The server owns the inventory. The client only ever asks

items.title: Gun System
items.short: A first person gun system on its own viewmodel rig. Forced first person, arms that match the avatar, spring recoil, surface sampling impacts, and every shot raycast again on the server.
body: A first person gun system built from scratch on its own viewmodel rig rather than a stock Roblox tool. Equipping locks the camera into first person and spawns a set of arms only you can see, animated separately from the character so the slide cycles and the magazine drops on their own timing. The client raycasts the instant you click so the shot feels immediate, and the server raycasts again before any of it counts.

The system is split by ownership rather than crammed into one script. GunServer holds the magazine, the reserve, the fire rate, and all damage, and hands the tool out on spawn. GunClient lives inside the tool and owns everything the player feels, the viewmodel, the animations, the camera recoil, and the input. GunThirdPerson runs on every other client and draws what everyone else sees, so a shot never renders twice for the person who fired it.

Shared code sits in the middle. GunConfig holds every number in one place, from fire rate and spread to recoil and particle counts, so tuning never means opening a script. GunEffects owns muzzle flash, shell ejection, bullet holes, and impact particles, and the shooter and the spectators call the same functions. Ammo rides on player attributes instead of a remote, so the HUD updates itself without anything having to ask.
features: Forced first person on equip, released the moment the gun is put away
Viewmodel arms that copy the skin tone and clothing of the avatar, so the hands on screen match the character
Four animations driven on the gun itself, equip, idle, reload, and fire, with the slide and magazine rigged as their own bones
Reload length read from the audio file at runtime and the animation speed scaled to match, so the two never drift apart
Camera recoil that kicks and settles on a spring, with a spread cone that widens per shot and decays back down
Impact particles that sample the colour of whatever surface they hit, switching to blood on anything with a humanoid
Ejected brass that bounces and despawns, and bullet holes that skip characters entirely
Dry fire click on an empty magazine, and a reload that cancels cleanly if the gun is put away part way through
Ammo counter and crosshair that show themselves only while the gun is out
architecture: Server: GunServer owns ammo, fire rate, and damage, and re-raycasts every shot rather than trusting the one it was handed
Shared: GunConfig for tuning, GunEffects for anything visual, and a viewmodel rig stored ready to clone
Client: GunClient inside the tool for the holder, GunThirdPerson for everyone else, and a HUD script that reveals itself only when armed
Four dedicated remotes rather than one catch all, so equipping, reloading, and firing are each validated on their own terms
The viewmodel is parented to the camera, so it renders for the holder and never replicates to anybody else
It sits in its own collision group, because the Humanoid it needs in order to wear clothing forces its torso to collide and would otherwise shove the player around
Shots are thrown out if they start more than fourteen studs from the character, or arrive faster than the fire rate allows

code.caption: Every number the gun runs on, in one file. Tuning never means opening a script.
lines: Config.FireDelay = 60 / 450 -- 450 rpm ceiling, semi auto still needs a floor between clicks
Config.Spread = 0.4 -- degrees of cone at rest
Config.SpreadPerShot = 0.5 -- added per shot, decays back to Config.Spread
Config.ReloadTimeFallback = 2.2 -- only used if the reload sound never reports a length
-- the rig's head sits 1.5 studs above its root, so dropping the root by that much puts the head
-- exactly on the camera. it is raised a little off that to lift the gun out of the bottom edge.
-- this is the knob to turn if the gun sits too high or low on screen
Pitch = 0.32, -- degrees of upward kick per shot
Yaw = 0.1, -- degrees of sideways kick per shot, sign is random
Speed = 26, -- how fast the kick lands
Return = 11, -- how fast it settles back to centre

items.title: Crate Opening System
items.short: A crate opening system that plays as a full cinematic rather than a menu popup. Three crates, spring driven camera work, a scrolling knife strip, and a server that picks the result before the animation ever starts.
body: A crate opening system where each crate sits on a stand and opens with a full cinematic instead of a menu popup. You walk up, hold E, and the camera moves in on the crate while a panel slides out with the drop table. When you open it, the crate lifts, spins up, slams back down and throws its lid open. Then a strip of knives scrolls across the screen and lands on what you won. The server picks the knife before any of that starts, so the animation only ever shows a result that already exists.

The code is split by who owns what. CrateService takes the request, checks distance, cooldown and balance, then charges the player, rolls and saves. DataService handles profiles with session locking, so two servers never write the same save. On the client, OpeningController runs the sequence in five acts and hands pieces off to smaller parts. CrateRig moves the crate and swings the lid on its hinge, Spinner builds and runs the strip, and RevealStage puts the knife on show.
The odds live in one shared module that both sides use. The server rolls with it and the drop table reads from it, so the percentages a player sees are the exact numbers the server uses.
features: Three crates with their own odds, prices and seam glow, on stands that sway slowly and peek their lids open every few seconds
Camera moves run on springs, with shake that builds while the crate charges and a kick when it bursts
The strip ticks each time a card passes the marker, and the ticks drop in pitch as it slows
Near misses get placed right next to lower tier wins, the same way real case openings do it
Space skips the strip by easing straight to the result instead of cutting to it
The knife reveal has a light, rays and sparkles colored by rarity, with Godly cycling through the whole rainbow
Duplicates stack, with a NEW badge on the first copy and an owned count after that
15 knives and 3 crates modeled in Blender, plus 36 sound effects made from scratch for this project
architecture: Server: CrateService and GemService validate everything, and DataService owns saving and only sends the fields that changed
Shared: config for rarities, crates, knives and the economy, plus Odds, Spring, Easing, Signal and Trove
Client: one controller per job (Shop, Opening, Stand, Camera, Hud, Prompt, Sound and Data)
Each crate is posed with a single BulkMoveTo per frame instead of welds or tweens on every part
The filler cards on the strip are rolled from the same crate odds, so the strip never shows fake rarities
Opens get rejected from more than 32 studs away, faster than the cooldown, or without enough gems to pay

code.caption: The rarity table both sides read from. Frozen at runtime so nothing can edit the tiers.
lines: export type Rarity = { -- shape every tier has to follow
Tier: number, -- higher number means rarer
Color: Color3, -- main color used on borders and lights
Light: Color3, -- lighter version for text and highlights
Dark: Color3, -- darker version for card backgrounds
Sound: string, -- name of the reveal sound in SoundService
Shake: number, -- how hard the camera shakes on reveal
Flash: boolean, -- turns on the screen flash and the banner
Rainbow: boolean, -- only godly uses this
local function rgb(r: number, g: number, b: number): Color3 -- just keeps the table below shorter
local byName: { [string]: Rarity } = { -- every tier looked up by its name
Color = rgb(178, 192, 212), -- plain grey so it never steals focus
Flash = false, -- rare still has to earn the flash
Flash = true, -- first tier that gets the banner
Color = rgb(255, 58, 106), -- fallback color for anything that cant do rainbow
Shake = 0.85, -- as loud as the camera gets
local order = { "Common", "Uncommon", "Rare", "Legendary", "Godly" } -- lowest to highest for anything that loops tiers
local rainbow = ColorSequence.new({ -- full hue sweep for godly text and glows
local function gradient(rarity: Rarity): ColorSequence -- builds the gradient the ui puts on rarity text
return rainbow -- godly skips the normal fade
ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, rarity.Light), -- bright at the top
ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, rarity.Color:Lerp(rarity.Dark, 0.35)), -- a little darker at the bottom for depth
return table.freeze({ -- frozen so nothing can edit the tiers at runtime
